definition: A major part of a company's business that it reports on separately, usually a product line or region. Companies show revenue and profit for each segment so investors can see which parts drive results. "Customer segment" or "market segment" means a group of customers instead.
The yearly report every U.S. public company must file with the SEC. It describes the business, its risks and its full-year audited financial statements.
The U.S. government agency that regulates stock markets and public companies. It sets disclosure rules and collects filings like the 10-K.
The quarterly report public companies file with the SEC for each of the first three quarters of the year. It's a shorter, unaudited version of the 10-K.
A report public companies file with the SEC within a few days of a major event, such as an acquisition, a CEO change or a bankruptcy.
Permission to use something someone else owns, such as a patent, brand or software, usually in exchange for a fee or royalty.
Combined into one set of numbers. Consolidated financial statements add up the parent company and all the subsidiaries it controls as if they were a single company.
The money a company takes in from selling its products and services, before subtracting any costs. Also called sales or the "top line".
A government grant giving an inventor the exclusive right to make, use and sell an invention for a limited time, usually 20 years from filing.
A company's employees and their skills, experience and knowledge, treated as a resource. 10-Ks have a human capital section about headcount, hiring, pay and culture.
A company that is controlled by another company (its parent), usually because the parent owns more than half of its shares. "Wholly owned" means the parent owns 100%.
When one company buys another company, or a business unit or asset of it, and takes control of it.
A legally protected name, logo, slogan or symbol that identifies a company's products, such as a brand name. Others can't use it without permission.
Item 1A of a 10-K: the company's list of things that could hurt its business or stock price. Companies must disclose the material ones.
Creations of the mind that the law protects as property: patents, trademarks, copyrights and trade secrets.
Everything a company owns or controls that has value, such as cash, buildings, equipment, inventory, patents and money owed to it.
A legal way of including another document's contents by pointing to it instead of copying it in. The referenced text counts as part of the filing.
Spending on creating new products and technologies or improving existing ones, such as lab work, engineering and testing.
The Securities Exchange Act of 1934, the U.S. law that created the SEC and requires public companies to file regular reports like the 10-K.
The whole network of suppliers, factories, warehouses and shippers involved in getting a product from raw materials to the customer.
The rules and practices for how a company is directed and controlled, including how the board oversees management and protects shareholders.
The people and institutions that own a company's shares, and so own part of the company.
A business that buys products from manufacturers and resells them, usually to retailers or other businesses rather than to consumers.
Computer systems that do tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognizing images or making predictions.
Goods a company holds to sell, plus the materials and partly finished products it will use to make them.
Negotiation between an employer and a labor union over pay, hours and working conditions. The resulting contract is a collective bargaining agreement.
Basic materials a company buys to make its products, such as steel, cotton, chemicals or crops.
The highest-ranking manager in a company, responsible for overall strategy and operations. The CEO reports to the board of directors.
A business that two or more companies own and run together, sharing its costs, profits and risks, while staying separate companies.
Legal protection for original creative works such as software code, books, music and films, giving the owner the exclusive right to copy and distribute them.
Valuable business information kept confidential, such as a recipe, formula or process. It's protected as long as it stays secret, without being registered.
Money spent on long-lasting physical assets like buildings, factories, equipment and data centers, as opposed to day-to-day expenses.
Selling goods in large quantities to other businesses, such as retailers, rather than to individual consumers.
Lawsuits and other legal disputes handled through the courts.
Protecting computer systems, networks and data from attacks, theft and damage.
Long-term shifts in global temperatures and weather, mainly caused by greenhouse gas emissions. 10-Ks discuss its physical risks and the regulations it brings.
A building full of computer servers and networking equipment that stores data and runs applications and cloud services.
Regular, predictable swings in a business over the year, such as retailers selling most during the holidays.
A tax a government charges on imported (or sometimes exported) goods, which raises their cost.
The 12-month period a company uses for its accounts. It doesn't have to match the calendar year; Apple's, for example, ends in late September.
A document sent to shareholders before the annual meeting describing what they'll vote on, including board members and executive pay.
A contract to use property or equipment owned by someone else for a set time in exchange for regular payments.
Something that lets a company do better than its rivals, such as lower costs, a strong brand, patents or a large network of customers.
Legal phrasing for a harm big enough to matter significantly to the company's business, finances or results.
The process of finding and buying the goods and services a business (or government) needs.
A general rise in prices over time, which raises costs and reduces what money can buy.
A company whose main purpose is to own other companies (its subsidiaries) rather than to sell products itself. Berkshire Hathaway and Alphabet are examples.
Item 7 of a 10-K, where management explains in its own words what drove the year's financial results and what it expects ahead.
The percentage of all sales in a market that one company captures.
The money moving into and out of a business over a period. Positive cash flow means more cash came in than went out.
A payment a company makes to its shareholders, usually in cash, out of its profits.
A company that makes the finished product sold under its brand, such as a carmaker or PC maker. Suppliers sell parts to OEMs.
Government restrictions on trade or financial dealings with certain countries, companies or people, usually for foreign policy reasons.
Gases such as carbon dioxide and methane that trap heat in the atmosphere. Companies report and try to cut their emissions of them.
In business, a network of products, partners, developers and customers built around a company's platform that make it more valuable together.
The senior executive in charge of a company's finances: accounting, budgeting, financial reporting and raising money.
Orders a company has received but not yet delivered, which give a hint of future revenue.
Total sales after subtracting returns, discounts and allowances. Many companies use it as their revenue figure.
What a company owes to others, such as loans, bonds, unpaid bills and other obligations. Also used for legal responsibility, as in product liability.
The ordinary shares of a company. They usually carry voting rights and a claim on profits, but are paid last if the company fails.
An arrangement where a company (franchisor) lets independent owners (franchisees) run businesses under its brand and system in exchange for fees.
A fossil fuel, mostly methane, used for heating, cooking and generating electricity.
Businesses that buy a company's products and sell them on to end customers, often adding their own services.
How easily a company can get cash to pay its short-term bills. Also how easily an asset can be sold without lowering its price.
Buying and selling goods and services online.
A business model where customers pay a recurring fee (monthly or yearly) for ongoing access to a product or service.
The U.S. federal agency that writes and enforces rules on air and water pollution, chemicals and waste.
A company's chief lawyer, who leads its legal department.
Statements about the future, such as plans, forecasts and expectations. Companies label them so they have legal protection if things turn out differently.
Materials that can harm people or the environment, such as certain chemicals and waste, which the law strictly regulates.
When a company buys back its own shares from the market, reducing the number of shares and returning cash to shareholders.
Energy from sources that don't run out, such as solar, wind and hydropower.
Relating to politics and relations between countries, such as wars, trade disputes and sanctions, and how they affect business.
Selling off or spinning off a business unit, subsidiary or asset.
When two companies combine to form one.
Major changes to a company's organization or operations to cut costs or refocus, such as layoffs, closing sites or reorganizing units.
Managing investments on behalf of clients, such as pension funds or individuals, for a fee.
Financial contracts whose value depends on something else, such as an interest rate, currency or commodity price. Often used to hedge risk.
Paying someone back. In healthcare, the payment a provider or drugmaker receives from insurers or government programs like Medicare.
A promise to repair or replace a product if it fails within a set period.
Laws that promote competition by banning monopolies, price-fixing and mergers that would hurt competition.
Evaluating and taking on risk for a fee. Insurers underwrite policies; banks underwrite stock and bond sales by guaranteeing to buy them.
A loan used to buy property, where the property serves as collateral the lender can take if the loan isn't repaid.
A U.S. law that bans companies from bribing foreign officials to win or keep business.
The total number of a company's products currently in use by customers. It drives sales of services, parts and upgrades.
Countries with fast-growing, developing economies, such as India, Brazil or Indonesia.
Hiring another company to do work that could be done in-house, such as manufacturing, IT or customer service.
Artificial intelligence that creates new content, such as text, images or code, from prompts. Chatbots built on large language models are an example.
A kind of artificial intelligence where computers learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules.
The European Union's main data privacy law. It controls how companies collect and use personal data about people in the EU.
The U.S. agency that enforces consumer protection and antitrust laws.
The U.S. agency that oversees financial products for consumers, such as mortgages, credit cards and loans.
Making an investment, often with derivatives, that offsets a risk, such as locking in a currency exchange rate or fuel price.
A material, usually silicon, used to make computer chips. "Semiconductors" also means the chips themselves.
A company hired by the main contractor on a project to do part of the work.
Selling straight to end customers, for example through a company's own stores or website, rather than through retailers or distributors.
A U.S. employer-sponsored retirement savings plan, often with employer matching contributions.
The largest U.S. stock exchange, where shares of many public companies trade.
A legal process for companies that can't pay their debts. Under Chapter 11, a company keeps operating while it reorganizes its debts.
A payment to the owner of a patent, brand, song or resource for the right to use it, often a percentage of sales.
Revenue minus the direct cost of making the goods sold, often shown as a percentage of revenue. It shows how profitable each sale is.
The profit left after subtracting all costs, interest and taxes from revenue. The "bottom line".
A grade from an agency such as Moody's or S&P on how likely a borrower is to repay its debts. Higher ratings mean cheaper borrowing.
The U.S. agency that sets and enforces workplace safety rules.
The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, a U.S. agency that insures bank deposits and supervises many banks.
Money of other countries. Companies that sell abroad see their results move as exchange rates change.
Laws and controls that stop criminals from disguising illegal money as legitimate, for example by requiring banks to check customers and report suspicious activity.
A large warehouse that receives goods and ships them on to stores or straight to customers.
How a company decides to use its cash: investing in the business, buying companies, paying down debt, paying dividends or buying back shares.
Relating to the economy as a whole, such as growth, inflation, interest rates and unemployment.
Profit from the core business: revenue minus operating costs, before interest and taxes.
Short-term assets (like cash, inventory and money customers owe) minus short-term liabilities (like bills due). It shows ability to fund day-to-day operations.
A financial statement listing what a company owns (assets), owes (liabilities) and the owners' stake (equity) on a given date.
A company that makes products for other companies, which then sell them under their own brands.
The U.S. agency that approves and regulates drugs, medical devices, food safety and more.
The U.S. central bank. It sets interest rate policy and supervises large banks and bank holding companies.
A broad 2010 U.S. law that tightened rules on banks and financial firms after the 2008 financial crisis.
A firm that buys and sells securities, both on behalf of customers (as a broker) and for itself (as a dealer).
Banking services for companies and governments, such as raising money by selling stocks and bonds, and advising on mergers.
Cleaning up pollution in soil, water or buildings, often required by law at old industrial sites.
Natural gas cooled into a liquid so it can be shipped long distances by tanker.
Sales of parts, repairs and services for products after the original sale, such as spare engine parts.
Outside companies, such as resellers and distributors, that sell or help sell a company's products.
A reseller that bundles a company's products with its own services, such as installation or customization.
A retirement plan that pays former employees a regular income after they retire.
A credit rating of BBB- (or Baa3) or higher, meaning the borrower is seen as relatively safe and can borrow more cheaply.
Shares that usually pay a fixed dividend and get paid before common stock, but typically don't carry voting rights.
Selling through several connected channels, such as stores, websites and apps, so customers can shop across them seamlessly.
Cost savings that come from being bigger: the more a company produces, the lower its cost per unit.

term: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
definition: The U.S. agency that charters and supervises national banks.
International banking rules that set how much capital and cash banks must hold to absorb losses.
A regulator's check of whether a bank could survive a severe economic downturn, using hypothetical crisis scenarios.
A company that owns or controls one or more banks. The Federal Reserve supervises it.
A bank holding company allowed to own a broader range of financial businesses, such as securities firms and insurers.
Insurance for insurance companies: an insurer passes part of its risk to a reinsurer in exchange for part of the premium.
The other side of a financial contract or trade, who could fail to pay what they owe.
A target of balancing any greenhouse gases a company emits with an equal amount removed, so its overall contribution is zero.
The U.S. law and program for cleaning up the most contaminated sites, which can make past and present owners pay for the cleanup.
Processing crude oil into products like gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
Unprocessed oil pumped from the ground, before it is refined into fuels and chemicals.
The U.S. government health insurance program for people 65 and older and some people with disabilities.
The U.S. health coverage program for people with low incomes, run jointly by the federal government and the states.
A company that runs prescription drug benefits for health plans and employers, negotiating drug prices and processing pharmacy claims.
Agreements to supply goods or services to a government. They come with special rules, audits and the right to cancel.
Generally accepted accounting principles: the standard accounting rules U.S. companies must use in their financial statements.
Things that make it hard for new competitors to enter a market, such as high startup costs, regulation or strong existing brands.
An accounting write-down when an asset is worth less than the value on the books, which shows up as a loss.
When a company turns one of its businesses into a separate public company, usually by giving the new company's shares to its own shareholders.
Someone legally required to act in another person's best interest, such as a trustee or an investment adviser managing a client's money.
Converting one currency into another, and the exchange rates used to do it.
Government rules that limit which goods and technology can be shipped to certain countries or buyers, often for national security.
A formal request by a regulated utility to the state regulator to change the prices it charges customers.
A company that owns income-producing real estate and pays out most of its taxable income as dividends, in exchange for not paying corporate income tax.
The later stages of a supply chain, closer to the customer. In oil and gas, refining and selling fuels.
A near copy of a biologic drug (one made from living cells), sold after the original's patents expire, like a generic for biologics.
The company that holds the main contract with the customer, often a government, and manages any subcontractors.
A measure of how much profit a company earns for each dollar invested in the business by shareholders and lenders.
The value delivered to a company's owners, mainly through a rising share price and dividends.
A major U.S. stock exchange known for listing many technology companies.
A promise to cover someone else's losses or legal costs in certain situations.
A promise in a loan or bond agreement, such as keeping debt below a set level. Breaking it can let lenders demand repayment.
Spreading the cost of an intangible asset, like a patent, over its useful life. Also paying off a loan gradually.
Spreading the cost of a physical asset, like a machine or building, over the years it is used, as it wears out.
The U.S. federal department that enforces federal law, including antitrust and anti-bribery laws.
Financial advice and investment services for wealthy individuals and families.
The total market value of the investments a firm manages for its clients.
The person or company that owns an insurance policy.
An insurance product that pays a stream of income, often for life, in exchange for an upfront payment or series of payments.
Bundling loans, such as mortgages or car loans, into securities that can be sold to investors.
The value of a regulated utility's investments on which regulators let it earn a set return through customer rates.
The early stages of a supply chain. In oil and gas, finding and producing crude oil and natural gas.
A research study testing a new drug or medical device in people to see if it is safe and effective, usually run in phases 1 to 3.
A period when a drug or product is legally protected from competing copies, through patents or regulatory rules.
When a drug's patents or exclusivity period end and cheaper generic or biosimilar copies can be sold, usually cutting its sales sharply.
Health coverage provided by private insurers, often through employers, as opposed to government programs like Medicare and Medicaid.
A factory that manufactures computer chips designed by other companies.
A chip company that designs semiconductors but outsources their manufacturing to foundries.
A thin disc of silicon on which many computer chips are made at once before being cut apart.
Servicing equipment, especially aircraft and engines, to keep it safe and working.
Paying employees with company shares or options to buy shares, in addition to salary.
Financial measures that don't follow standard accounting rules (GAAP), such as profit excluding one-time costs. Companies must show how they reconcile to GAAP.
A company connected to another through ownership or control, such as a parent, subsidiary or sister company.
Owned exclusively by the company, such as its own technology or processes, which others can't freely use.
A country, state or other area with its own laws and courts, or the authority to apply them.
A basic raw material traded in bulk that's interchangeable no matter who produces it, such as oil, copper, wheat or coffee.
A company's profit. Usually means net income.
How much and how quickly a price or value swings up and down.
An independent business that sells a manufacturer's products, such as a car dealership.
The radio frequencies used for wireless communication. Carriers buy licenses to use specific bands from the government.
Net income divided by the number of shares: how much profit the company made for each share.
Cash generated by operations minus capital expenditures: the cash left over to pay dividends, buy back shares or pay down debt.
Owning several stages of the supply chain, such as making parts, assembling products and selling them, instead of relying on other companies.
Revenue that comes in regularly and predictably, such as from subscriptions or service contracts.
Software delivered over the internet on a subscription instead of installed and bought outright.
Environmental, social and governance: factors investors use to judge a company's sustainability and ethics, such as emissions, labor practices and board oversight.
A stock market index of about 500 of the largest U.S. public companies, widely used as a benchmark for the market.
Finding, recruiting and hiring employees.
Winning new customers, and the cost of doing so through marketing and sales.
Short-term IOUs, usually due within 270 days, that large companies sell to investors to fund day-to-day needs.
A pre-arranged loan a company can draw on, repay and draw again up to a limit, like a corporate credit card.
